skin.setting: an excavation house in the Valley of the Kings, 1922
skin.title: The Valley Scribe's Demise
skin.place: An archaeological base camp in the Valley of the Kings
skin.styleGuide: Sun-bleached sepia tones, dusty limestone textures, vintage gelatin silver photography feel, and deep amber lantern-lit shadows.

rooms.name: the Darkroom
rooms.description: A windowless chamber sealed against the harsh desert light, reeking of hypo and silver nitrate.

rooms.name: the Vestibule
rooms.description: The main entry foyer with whitewashed mudbrick walls and hooks for pith helmets and linen dusters.

rooms.name: the Office
rooms.description: The expedition leader's headquarters, lined with site maps, specimen jars, and wooden filing cabinets.

rooms.name: the Veranda
rooms.description: An open stone terrace looking out over the desolate limestone cliffs under the starry desert night.

rooms.name: the Drafting Room
rooms.description: A spacious workroom fitted with wide drafting tables, drawing ink bottles, and architectural section drawings.

rooms.name: the Central Courtyard
rooms.description: An airy courtyard covered with canvas shades, providing passage between the wings of the dig house.

rooms.name: the Artifact Storage
rooms.description: A reinforced storeroom packed with numbered crates, straw padding, and newly cataloged potsherds.

rooms.name: the Field Lab
rooms.description: A narrow laboratory fitted with balance scales, preservation chemicals, and cleaning brushes.

people.name: Arthur Pendelton
people.bio: A meticulous scholar of Middle Egyptian hieroglyphs who spent years deciphering tomb inscriptions. He felt his academic contributions were routinely overshadowed and claimed by Lord Croft.
people.voice: Speaks with quiet, clipped academic precision and an air of weary resignation.
people.motive: Lord Croft was preparing to publish Arthur's groundbreaking translation under his own name.
people.portrait: A lean, sharp-featured man in his late thirties with thinning dark hair, rimless spectacles, and a sun-faded khaki linen suit.

people.name: Evelyn Mercer
people.bio: A skilled draftswoman responsible for rendering delicate tomb murals and pottery motifs. Her contract was abruptly threatened with cancellation following a bitter aesthetic dispute.
people.voice: Speaks in measured, composed tones with a sharp undercurrent of defiance.
people.motive: Lord Croft threatened to dismiss her without pay and blacklist her from future museum expeditions.
people.portrait: A slender woman in her late twenties with dark hair pinned back neatly, wearing a charcoal waistcoat over a high-collared white blouse.

people.name: Dr. Julian Sterling
people.bio: A veteran archaeologist whose rival excavation methods were widely criticized by modern theorists. He had financed part of the season in exchange for co-director credit.
people.voice: Speaks in a haughty, aristocratic cadence laced with condescension.
people.motive: Lord Croft intended to publicly expel him from the excavation team over disputed artifact provenance.
people.portrait: A stout, broad-shouldered gentleman in his fifties with silvered temples, a bristling mustache, and a heavy tweed waistcoat.

people.name: Farouk Al-Masri
people.bio: A respected local leader managing the workforce of regional diggers and haulers. He had repeatedly clashed with the leadership over severe wage cuts and dangerous tunnel conditions.
people.voice: Speaks firmly and courteously in resonant, measured English with Arabic cadence.
people.motive: Lord Croft had withheld the promised seasonal bonuses from the local digging crews.
people.portrait: A tall, weathered man in his forties with commanding posture, deep-set brown eyes, and a crisp white galabeya with an embroidered vest.

people.name: Beatrice Vance
people.bio: An eccentric heiress whose family foundation poured thousands of pounds into the dig season. She discovered her funds were being secretly diverted into speculative private ventures.
people.voice: Speaks with a dry, drawling theatricality that masks a calculating intellect.
people.motive: Lord Croft had embezzled a substantial portion of her endowment for personal financial speculation.
people.portrait: An imposing woman in her forties with striking cheekbones, tightly curled auburn hair, and an elegant tailored travel gown.

people.name: Thomas Finch
people.bio: A technical specialist who documented every stage of the tomb clearance with heavy glass plates. He held quiet resentment over dangerous assignments in unventilated burial shafts.
people.voice: Speaks in a hurried, nervous whisper, constantly checking his surroundings.
people.motive: Lord Croft forced him to alter photographic documentation to conceal the accidental destruction of tomb reliefs.
people.portrait: A wiry young man with disheveled sandy hair, ink-stained cuffs, and a dust-coated twill vest over a rumpled linen shirt.

people.name: Lord Alistair Croft
people.bio: A charismatic but ruthless explorer who claimed sole glory for the team's archaeological discoveries. His domineering management alienated nearly everyone under his command.
people.voice: Speaks with booming, unquestioned authority and little patience for dissent.
people.portrait: A tall, aristocratic man in his early fifties with a stern jaw, slicked grey hair, and a bespoke safari jacket with brass buttons.

I have told you all that I know. My sketches occupied all of my attention.

The deceased lies motionless, offering no answers to the investigators.
skin.briefing: On the dry, windblown evening of November 14, 1922, the tranquil routine of the Valley of the Kings expedition house was shattered. Lord Alistair Croft, the celebrated and domineering director of the excavation, was discovered dead in his private office, slain by a heavy limestone surveying marker. The perimeter remained secured against outside intruders, confirming the murderer is among the six members of the inner expedition circle present in the compound. The killer will lie to evade the gallows, while the innocent scholars and staff speak the absolute truth.
skin.scene: A low-slung mudbrick expedition house under the starry night sky of the Valley of the Kings, amber oil lantern glow spilling from open doorways onto sun-baked desert sand.
skin.summingUp:
The dust of this old limestone room settles under the amber glow of the lanterns, fixed like a faded silver plate in the dark. We know that Lord Alistair Croft met his end in the Office, and the timeline leaves no room for doubt. To begin with, the murder was not at 5:00 PM or Midnight, because Card 6 narrows down when the murder happened. Furthermore, Dr. Julian Sterling must have been in the Office at 8:00 PM, because Card 12 puts the two of them in one room. By that exact same token, Farouk Al-Masri must have been in the Office at 8:00 PM, because Card 12 puts the two of them in one room. From this, Thomas Finch is in the clear, because the killer and Lord Alistair Croft were both in the Office when it happened.

Look closely at that eight o'clock hour. At 8:00 PM it was none of Arthur Pendelton, Evelyn Mercer, Farouk Al-Masri, or Beatrice Vance, because Dr. Julian Sterling can only have been in the Office then, and the one living soul in that room was the killer. That rules out Arthur Pendelton at 6:00 PM, Arthur Pendelton at 7:00 PM, Evelyn Mercer at 6:00 PM, Evelyn Mercer at 7:00 PM, Farouk Al-Masri at 6:00 PM, Farouk Al-Masri at 7:00 PM, Beatrice Vance at 6:00 PM, and Beatrice Vance at 7:00 PM, because Dr. Julian Sterling was in the Office, and after the murder nobody but the killer was. Consequently, the murder was not at 8:00 PM, because Farouk Al-Masri can only have been in the Office then, and the one living soul in that room was the killer. Nor could it have occurred earlier: the murder was not at 6:00 PM or 7:00 PM, because Farouk Al-Masri was in the Office, and after the murder nobody but the killer was.

The remaining possibilities crumble under scrutiny. Evelyn Mercer is in the clear, because supposing it was Evelyn Mercer leaves nothing that fits. Dr. Julian Sterling is in the clear, because supposing it was Dr. Julian Sterling leaves nothing that fits. Turning to the later hours, the murder was not at 10:00 PM, because supposing the murder happened at 10:00 PM leaves nothing that fits. Likewise, the murder was not at 11:00 PM, because supposing the murder happened at 11:00 PM leaves nothing that fits.

Thus, Arthur Pendelton and Farouk Al-Masri are in the clear, because there is no way for Beatrice Vance to have been innocent. It was Beatrice Vance, striking at 9:00 PM in the Office, driven by the discovery that Lord Croft had embezzled a substantial portion of her endowment for personal financial speculation.
